refnamediv.refpurpose: Home area/user account manager configuration files

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: These configuration files control default parameters for home areas/user accounts created and managed by systemd-homed.service8.

refsect1.title: Options
refsect1.para: The following options are available in the [Home] section:

listitem.para: The default storage to use for home areas. Takes one of luks, fscrypt, directory, subvolume, cifs. For details about these options, see homectl1. If not configured or assigned the empty string, the default storage is automatically determined: if not running in a container environment and /home/ is not itself encrypted, defaults to luks. Otherwise, defaults to subvolume if /home/ is on a btrfs file system, and directory otherwise. Note that the storage selected on the homectl command line always takes precedence.

When using luks as storage (see above), selects the default file system to use inside the user's LUKS volume. Takes one of btrfs, ext4 or xfs. If not specified, defaults to btrfs. This setting has no effect if a different storage mechanism is used. The file system type selected on the homectl command line always takes precedence.

Configures the existing LVM thin pool used for newly created LUKS home areas that do not specify an explicit image path. The value must be a volume group and thin-pool name separated by a slash, for example homes/pool. Such homes use ext4. If no diskSize is specified, the logical size is derived from the current thin-pool data LV size plus the unallocated extents in its volume group, including space reserved for automatic pool extension, rounded down to the normal home-disk alignment and limited to the supported size range. An explicit diskSize remains authoritative, and may be used to impose a lower ceiling or deliberately overcommit the pool. Resizing and automatic space rebalancing are disabled for these fixed logical devices. The ext4 file system is mounted in provisioning mode, so allocation fails before a mapping is exposed unless the complete block stack can back it. Online discard is enabled by default for these block-device-backed homes; the thin pool and all lower block layers must also be configured to pass discards down for unused extents to be reclaimed. systemd-homed creates and removes only tagged per-user thin volumes in this pool, and records the pool, volume name, and immutable LVM volume UUID in the machine-specific user-record binding. Creating, monitoring, and sizing the pool remains an administrator responsibility.
The pool must use immediate error-on-full behavior. Configure a new pool along these lines, adjusting sizes and devices for the installation:
listitem.programlisting: pvcreate /dev/disk/by-id/… vgcreate homes /dev/disk/by-id/… lvcreate --type thin-pool --name pool --size 900G --poolmetadatasize 8G homes lvchange --errorwhenfull y --monitor y homes/pool
listitem.para: Before creating or activating a home, systemd-homed verifies that the configured volume is a writable, healthy thin pool, that it returns allocation errors instead of queuing I/O indefinitely when full, and that neither its data nor metadata space is exhausted. It warns when either usage reaches 80%, and when dmeventd monitoring is disabled. Configure LVM thin-pool auto-extension, keep unallocated extents in the volume group for it, and monitor both data_percent and metadata_percent. Metadata space needs to be sized for the expected number of thin devices, snapshots, and block mappings; exhausting it is as serious as exhausting data space.

Discard must be enabled through ext4, LUKS/device-mapper, the thin pool, and the backing storage. Verify reclamation by comparing lvs -o data_percent before and after fstrim; do not assume deleting files alone releases thin-pool blocks. If the pool becomes full, extend its data or metadata LV before retrying activation. For a check-needed, read-only, or failed pool, keep homes inactive and follow the LVM thin-pool repair procedure (normally including a metadata backup and lvconvert --repair). Do not rename, retag, or remove homed-owned thin LVs manually, since their immutable LVM UUIDs are part of the authenticated home binding.

Takes a boolean and defaults to false. When enabled, newly created thin-backed LUKS/ext4 homes use a hardware-wrapped inline-encryption key. The complete block stack and storage controller must support hardware-wrapped key generation, software-secret derivation, ephemeral-key preparation, inline AES-256-XTS encryption through dm-inlinecrypt, and journaled dm-integrity provisioning. The resulting stack is ext4 over dm-integrity, dm-inlinecrypt, and the LVM thin volume. Integrity uses an internal hmac(sha256) over filesystem plaintext with 4096-byte sectors, 32-byte tags, colocated metadata, and a fixed 32 MiB journal. The lower inline-encryption layer encrypts the data, integrity tags, superblock, and journal. An explicit yes fails creation if any required component is unavailable; it never falls back to a raw volume key. Existing wrapped homes remain usable when this setting is later disabled. This is intentionally a system-wide creation policy; no per-user homectl override is provided. New raw-key homes continue to use the unversioned identity-token format for compatibility, while version 2 is reserved for the authenticated hardware-wrapped-key envelope.

The wrapped key is tied to the storage hardware's wrapping identity. A LUKS header backup and the user's password are not sufficient for recovery after incompatible storage-controller or motherboard replacement. Keep normal LUKS header and LVM metadata backups for repair, but also keep an independent encrypted file-level backup. Migrate a home while the source hardware is available by unlocking it and copying its files into a newly created home on the destination; copying only the thin LV or LUKS header to hardware with a different wrapping identity is not a migration method.

Password, recovery-key, PKCS#11, and FIDO2 enrollment changes update normal LUKS2 keyslots while retaining the same wrapped data key. Online LUKS reencryption and data-key rotation are not supported for this profile. Locking a newly created wrapped home requires cryptsetup, a dm-inlinecrypt target version 1.1 or newer, and a dm-integrity target version 1.15 or newer with suspended key wipe/key set support. Older stacks return an unsupported-operation error without leaving only one layer resumed; full deactivation remains supported and evicts both active keys.

Each protected home permanently reserves approximately 32 MiB for the integrity journal, in addition to dm-integrity tags and filesystem blocks provisioned in the thin pool. Size thin-pool data and metadata capacity for this overhead. Homes created before integrity support retain their existing layout and do not acquire this reservation automatically.
